title: Wheelbarrow
wiki_lead:
A wheelbarrow is a small hand-propelled load-bearing vehicle, usually with just one wheel, designed to be pushed and guided by a single person using two handles at the rear. The term "wheelbarrow" is made of two words: "wheel" and "barrow." "Barrow" is a derivation of the Old English "barew" which was a device used for carrying loads.
The wheelbarrow is designed to distribute the weight of its load between the wheel and the operator, so enabling the convenient carriage of heavier and bulkier loads than would be possible were the weight carried entirely by the operator. As such it is a second-class lever. Traditional Chinese wheelbarrows, however, had a central wheel supporting the whole load. Use of wheelbarrows is common in the construction industry and in gardening. Typical capacity is approximately 100 litres (3.53 cubic feet) of material.
A two-wheel type is more stable on level ground, while the almost universal one-wheel type has better maneuverability in small spaces, on planks, in water, or when tilted ground would throw the load off balance. The use of one wheel also permits greater control of the deposition of the load upon emptying.

History


China

The earliest wheelbarrows with archaeological evidence in the form of a one-wheel cart come from second-century Han dynasty Emperor Hui's (d. 188 BC) tomb murals and brick tomb reliefs. The painted tomb mural of a man pushing a wheelbarrow was found in a tomb at Chengdu, Sichuan province, dated precisely to 118 AD. The stone carved relief of a man pushing a wheelbarrow was found in the tomb of Shen Fujun in Sichuan province, dated circa 150 AD. And then there is the story of the pious Dong Yuan pushing his father around in a single-wheel luche barrow, depicted in a mural of the Wu Liang tomb-shrine of Shandong (dated to AD 147). Earlier accounts dating to the 1st century BC and 1st century AD that mention a "deer cart" (鹿車, luche) might also have been referencing a wheelbarrow.
The 5th-century Book of Later Han stated that the wife of the once poor and youthful imperial censor Bao Xuan helped him push a lu che back to his village during their feeble wedding ceremony, around 30 BC. Later, during the Red Eyebrows Rebellion (c. 20 AD) against Xin dynasty's Wang Mang (45 BC–23 AD), the official Zhao Xi saved his wife from danger by disguising himself and pushing her along in his lu che barrow, past a group of brigand rebels who questioned him, and allowed him to pass after he convinced them that his wife was terribly ill. The first recorded description of a wheelbarrow appears in Liu Xiang's work Lives of Famous Immortals. Liu describes the invention of the wheelbarrow by the legendary Chinese mythological figure Ko Yu, who builds a "Wooden ox".
Nevertheless, the Chinese historical text of the Sanguozhi (Records of the Three Kingdoms), compiled by the ancient historian Chen Shou (233–297 AD), credits the invention of the wheelbarrow to Prime Minister Zhuge Liang (181–234 AD) of Shu Han from 197–234. It was written that in 231 AD, Zhuge Liang developed the vehicle of the wooden ox and used it as a transport for military supplies in a campaign against Cao Wei.


Centrally mounted wheel

Further annotations of the text by Pei Songzhi (430 AD) described the design in detail as a large single central wheel and axle around which a wooden frame was constructed in representation of an ox. Writing later in the 11th century, the Song dynasty (960–1279) scholar Gao Cheng wrote that the small wheelbarrow of his day, with shafts pointing forward (so that it was pulled), was the direct descendant of Zhuge Liang's wooden ox.  Furthermore, he pointed out that the third century 'gliding horse' wheelbarrow featured the simple difference of the shaft pointing backwards (so that it was pushed instead).

grok_lead: A wheelbarrow is a small, usually single-wheeled vehicle designed for carrying loads, fitted with handles at the rear for pushing and guiding by a single person. This simple yet efficient tool combines the principles of the wheel and lever, allowing one individual to transport heavier materials than would be feasible by hand alone, such as soil, gravel, tools, or supplies. The wheelbarrow's origins trace back to ancient China, where it was invented sometime between 100 and 230 CE during the early Common Era, marking a significant advancement in manual transportation. Earliest references attribute its development to the semi-legendary figure Ko Yu in the 1st century BCE, though practical designs emerged later, with improvements credited to the military strategist Zhuge Liang around 231 CE, who adapted it for efficient supply transport during wartime. In China, wheelbarrows were ingeniously varied, including models with large central wheels for balance and even sail-assisted versions using junk-style sails to harness wind power, which became a widespread technology for agriculture and logistics over millennia. These early forms often featured the wheel positioned centrally under the load for optimal leverage, differing from later Western designs where the wheel is at the front. Wheelbarrows did not appear in Europe until the Middle Ages, with the earliest depiction in a 1220 CE stained-glass window at Chartres Cathedral, likely introduced via trade routes from Asia. Today, they remain essential in gardening, construction, farming, and trail maintenance, available in types such as traditional single-wheel models for maneuverability in tight spaces, two-wheeled variants for stability with heavier loads, and specialized designs like open-frame versions for hauling rocks or timber. Their enduring utility lies in their low cost, portability, and ability to navigate uneven terrain, making them a staple tool worldwide.
